# CRS required-literal prefilter: design, coverage and soundness

**Status:** experimental implementation, **not enabled by default**.
**Branch:** `perf/crs-prefilter` (worktree `.worktrees/crs-prefilter`), based on
`main` @ `cf9ba16`.
**Date:** 2026-11-02
**Engine:** Coraza `v3.3.3`, OWASP CRS `4.14.0` (vendored bundle), PL1.
**Artifact:** `rules/crs/prefilter.json` (schema v1), generated by
`cargo run --features crs-prefilter --bin crs-prefilter-extract`.

## TL;DR

The prefilter is **sound by construction**: it only skips body evaluation when
every body-relevant CRS rule has a *proven* required literal and none of those
literals occurs in the body (under every representation a CRS rule can see).
Anything the extractor cannot prove is marked `ungated`, and the native mode
falls back to full CRS.

On the stock CRS 4.14 bundle at paranoia level 1 the fast path is **not
available**: 62 of 113 body-relevant entries are gated after extraction. The
ungated set includes `@detectSQLi` (942100), the obfuscation-tolerant 932
regexes (932250/932260/932230/932235), several 942 rules whose alternations
contain short keywords, and the numeric/validation protocol checks. Because the
mode requires *all* body-relevant rules to be gated, `BodyWithhold` never fires
on stock CRS. That is the correct, conservative outcome; the report below
quantifies what is missing and what the next integration step should be.

The prefilter itself costs ~1.4-2.0 ms/KiB (release, 84 automata) and hits
47 % of the benign corpus. The hits are common-substring false positives
(`ord` inside `password`, short SQL keywords in prose), not CRS matches. A
clean result is a proof, so it is safe to run in `DryRun` mode on any rule set
for measurement; the hit rate and the per-request cost are the two levers to
tune before a per-rule integration.

## Update: per-rule gating (implemented)

Per-rule gating has landed behind `waf.coraza.prefilter = "gated"` (default
`off`). Instead of withholding the body, the host scans **every request
representation** — method, URI, query string, header names/values, cookies and
body — with the same automata and removes only the gated rules whose mandatory
literals are absent from all of them. Ungated rules always run, so the decision
is unchanged on stock CRS.

* The Rust host computes the list with `Prefilter::evaluate_request` (bounded
  to `MAX_REMOVE_RULE_IDS = 256`) and `sanitize_remove_rule_ids`.
* The list travels as `remove_rule_ids` in the JSON envelope and as an optional
  section in binary v1, negotiated via handshake capability bits.
* Both guests validate every id against their own copy of
  `rules/crs/prefilter.json` (embedded in the WASI reactor, read next to
  `--rules` by the sidecar) and call `tx.RemoveRuleByID` before `ProcessURI`.
  A forged payload therefore cannot disable an ungated or unknown rule, and
  removal is per transaction.
* The vendored Coraza patch that exposes `RemoveRuleByID` on
  `types.Transaction` is in `patches/` and is re-applied by both Go build
  paths.

Measured on the pinned native sidecar (release, 5 reps, benign synthetic
bodies, stock CRS 4.14 PL1):

| body | off p50 | gated p50 | speedup | rules removed |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 KiB | 35.11 ms | 27.65 ms | 1.3x | 58 |
| 4 KiB | 39.43 ms | 26.24 ms | 1.5x | 58 |
| 8 KiB | 78.37 ms | 49.72 ms | 1.6x | 58 |
| 16 KiB | 148.71 ms | 96.02 ms | 1.5x | 58 |
| 60 KiB | 543.82 ms | 354.03 ms | 1.5x | 58 |

Detection parity on the 51-case corpus: **0 false negatives, 0 false
positives**. Benign corpus removal: 57.3 rules per request (of 61 distinct
gated ids; the remaining matches are literal false positives such as `ord` in
`password`). The prefilter scan itself is included in the gated timings.


## 1. What the prefilter does

For each body-relevant rule the offline extractor emits a **disjunctive
required-literal set**: every value that can match the rule contains at least
one member of the set. The runtime builds one Aho-Corasick automaton per
`(representation, transform pipeline, case sensitivity)` group and scans the
body. If no automaton matches, no gated rule can match any body-derived value.

```
body ──► extraction variants ──► transform pipeline ──► Aho-Corasick
         identity                (urlDecodeUni, ...)     (one per group)
         urlDecode
         jsonUnescape
         htmlEntityDecode
```

A hit only means "run full CRS". A miss is the proof used to withhold the body
(or, in a future integration, to remove the gated rules for the transaction).

### 1.1 Literal extraction

* `@pm` / `@pmFromFile`: the complete phrase list, lowercased. Coraza's
  `pm_from_file.go` trims, drops `#`/blank lines and matches ASCII
  case-insensitively, so the runtime uses an ASCII-case-insensitive automaton.
* `@rx`: a small PCRE parser computes a required-literal set:
  * literal runs are merged (`foo\.bar` → `foo.bar`),
  * alternations union their branch sets (`(?:wget|curl|nc)` →
    `{wget,curl,nc}`) **only if every branch yields a set**,
  * a branch whose only literal is shorter than 3 characters makes the whole
    alternation ungated (a match could use just that branch),
  * finite groups are expanded (`m(?:aster|s(?:db|ys))` → `master`, `msdb`,
    `mys`, ...) so a rule like 942140 can still be gated,
  * lookarounds, conditionals, backreferences, unknown escapes, byte-mode
    `\xHH` above 0x7F and unbounded repeats yield no literal.
* `@contains`/`@streq`/`@beginsWith`/`@endsWith`/`@within`: the literal argument.
* Negated operators (`!@rx`, `!@pm`, ...) are **never** gated: the rule matches
  on the *absence* of the pattern.
* `@detectSQLi`, `@detectXSS`, numeric comparisons and validation operators have
  no literal requirement and are always ungated.

### 1.2 Transforms

The runtime reproduces these Coraza transforms exactly: `lowercase`,
`uppercase`, `urlDecode`, `urlDecodeUni`, `removeNulls`, `replaceNulls`,
`compressWhitespace`, `removeWhitespace`, `trim`, `trimLeft`, `trimRight`,
`normalizePath`, `normalizePathWin`, `escapeSeqDecode`, `replaceComments`,
`jsDecode`, `cssDecode`. `utf8toUnicode` is the identity for the ASCII literals
the extractor accepts.

`htmlEntityDecode` is **not** reproduced exactly (Go's HTML5 named-entity table
is large and context-sensitive), so rules that use it are ungated. `base64Decode`,
`cmdLine`, `length`, `sha1`/`md5`/`hexEncode` and the parity transforms are also
ungated.

### 1.3 Representations

A CRS body processor may hand a rule a value that is not a raw substring of the
body: form values are URL-decoded, JSON strings are unescaped, XML/HTML text is
entity-decoded. The runtime therefore scans four extraction variants (`identity`,
`urlDecode`, `jsonUnescape`, `htmlEntityDecode`) crossed with the rule's
transform chain. Scanning extra representations can only create false positives,
never false negatives.

XML is special: a `<!DOCTYPE`/`<!ENTITY` declaration can expand to an arbitrary
string that is not present in the body, so the prefilter forces full evaluation
when either token appears. This is the one structural "indicator" outside the
literal automata.

## 2. Soundness argument

Let `R` be a gated body-relevant rule, `B` the raw body, and `V` a value that
CRS derives from `B` for one of `R`'s targets. `V` is obtained by zero or more
body-processor extractions followed by `R`'s transform chain `T`. The extractor
proves `R` has a set `S` such that every match of `R` contains some `s ∈ S`.
The runtime scans `E(B)` for every extraction `E ∈ {identity, urlDecode,
jsonUnescape, htmlEntityDecode}` followed by `T`.

1. **Extraction coverage.** Every body processor in the vendored Coraza is one
   of: identity (`REQUEST_BODY`, multipart parts), URL decoding (form),
   JSON string unescaping, or XML/HTML entity decoding. For XML, a DTD
   declaration forces full evaluation; without one, only predefined and
   numeric entities are decoded, which `htmlEntityDecode` covers. Therefore
   `V` is a substring of at least one scanned representation.
2. **Transform fidelity.** For every supported transform the Rust
   implementation is a port of the Coraza Go function, so the scanned
   representation equals `T(V)` for that extraction. Extra representations do
   not remove bytes that `T(V)` contains.
3. **Literal necessity.** If `R` matches `V`, `V` contains some `s ∈ S`. Since
   `s` is a byte substring of `V` and `V` is a substring of a scanned
   representation, the automaton matches that representation. Contrapositive:
   no hit ⇒ `R` cannot match any body-derived value.
4. **Fallback.** If any body-relevant rule is ungated, the native mode runs
   full CRS. If the body contains a DTD/entity declaration, it runs full CRS.

A hit is not a claim that the rule matches; it only means the proof failed.
This one-sided contract is why the mode is safe to enable before the corpus is
exhaustive.

### 2.1 Adversarial extraction cases covered by tests

* alternation with a short branch → ungated (`(?:select|se)`),
* optional literal → the other branch is still required (`(?:foo)?bar`),
* `*` branch → ungated (`(?:foo|bar)*`),
* lookahead is not trusted (`(?=foo)bar` → `bar`),
* escaped quotes and `\Q...\E`,
* byte-mode `\xff` → class, not a UTF-8 literal,
* `(?i)` case flag propagated to every literal,
* `utf8toUnicode` accepted only for ASCII literals,
* negated operators → ungated,
* chain members gated independently (a chain is gated only when every
  body-relevant member is),
* URL/JSON/HTML extraction and `lowercase`/`removeNulls`/`jsDecode`/`cssDecode`
  transforms,
* DTD/entity declaration forces full evaluation.

### 2.2 Non-body representations

Per-rule gating must also cover rules whose targets include `ARGS`,
`ARGS_NAMES`, `REQUEST_HEADERS`, `REQUEST_COOKIES`, `REQUEST_FILENAME`,
`QUERY_STRING`, `REQUEST_URI`, `FILES` and `MULTIPART_PART_HEADERS`. The host
scans each of those values independently: method, the full URI (path and
query), every header name and value (which includes `Cookie`), and the body
(which contains multipart parts and file names). Each value is transformed on
its own, never concatenated, because `replaceComments`, `normalizePath` and
`cmdLine` are not monotonic across value boundaries. A literal that is absent
from every value is therefore absent from every target, which is the same
one-sided proof as the body case. Rules whose targets cannot be covered this
way stay ungated and always run.

## 3. Coverage on CRS 4.14

Artifact generated at paranoia level 1 (the engine default). Higher-level rules
are excluded, because the sidecar skips them; regenerate with
`--paranoia-level N` if the deployment runs a higher PL.

| family | body-relevant entries | gated | ungated |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 920 protocol enforcement | 8 | 1 | 7 |
| 921 protocol attack | 6 | 3 | 3 |
| 922 multipart attack | 4 | 2 | 2 |
| 930 LFI | 3 | 1 | 2 |
| 931 RFI | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| 932 RCE | 16 | 3 | 13 |
| 933 PHP | 12 | 7 | 5 |
| 934 generic | 6 | 4 | 2 |
| 941 XSS | 25 | 19 | 6 |
| 942 SQLi | 20 | 10 | 10 |
| 943 session fixation | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| 944 Java | 7 | 6 | 1 |
| **total** | **113** | **62** | **51** |

The gated entries include the phrase-file rules (930120, 931110, 932120,
932160, 933160/170/180, 944130) and the XSS `<` gate for `@detectXSS`
(941100). The ungated entries are dominated by:

| rule | family | why it cannot be gated |
|---:|---|---|
| 932250/932260/932230/932235 | 932 | generated obfuscation-tolerant regexes: every command letter is followed by optional junk, so no contiguous literal is guaranteed |
| 942100 | 942 | `@detectSQLi` (libinjection) has no literal |
| 942320/942550/942190/942230 | 942 | branches with only punctuation or short keywords |
| 942151/942170/942290/942500/942540 | 942 | alternations containing 2-character SQL keywords/functions |
| 941160/941170/941210/941220/941310/941360 | 941 | short tag/attribute names or no literal |
| 930100/930110 | 930 | traversal regexes made of character classes |
| 934100/934160 | 934 | `t:base64Decode` chains |
| 920360/920370/920380 | 920 | numeric size checks (`@gt`), no literal |
| 920250/920270 | 920 | UTF-8/byte-range validation, no literal |
| 944150 | 944 | no literal in the regex |

The ungated entries dominate the known cost centres: 932 RCE is ~29 % of body
time, 942 SQLi ~21 %, 934 generic ~11.5 %, 921 ~10 %, 941 ~9 %, 933 ~6.6 %,
944 ~6 %. The top 932 rules (932250/932260/932230/932235) are generated
obfuscation-tolerant regexes: every command letter is followed by optional
junk, so no two letters form a guaranteed contiguous literal. They cannot be
gated by a substring automaton without a gapped-subsequence matcher.

## 4. Measurements

Machine: Intel i5-8400T (6 cores, 1.7/3.3 GHz), shared with other agents during
these runs (load average 15-28). Absolute numbers are indicative; the ratios
are the useful part.

### 4.1 Prefilter cost (release build)

Artifact load + automata build: **257 ms** for 84 automata. This is a
start-up cost, not a per-request cost. Per-request scan cost (release build,
84 automata, no early exit on benign bodies, p50/p95 over 3):

| body | p50 | p95 | µs/KiB |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 KiB | 1.37 ms | 4.16 ms | 1 371 |
| 4 KiB | 7.02 ms | 9.29 ms | 1 754 |
| 8 KiB | 15.87 ms | 20.19 ms | 1 983 |
| 16 KiB | 71.37 ms | 102.99 ms | 4 461 |
| 60 KiB | 115.15 ms | 117.69 ms | 1 919 |

The 16 KiB row is an outlier from host load (the shared machine had a load
average of 15-28); the per-KiB cost is ~1.4-2.0 ms. That is **not** free: on an
8 KiB body it is ~10 % of the full-CRS 155 ms. The number of automata is the
main lever: 4 extraction variants × ~21 transform pipelines = 84 passes.
Passing the request content type to `evaluate` (form/JSON/XML/multipart) would
cut this to 1-2 variants (2-4×). Early exit on the first hit already helps
attack traffic.

### 4.2 Full CRS vs body withheld (native sidecar, release)

The sidecar is the pinned Go build (`CGO_ENABLED=0`, release), CRS 4.14 at PL1,
`--max-body 1048576`, p50/p95 over 3 evaluations. "Withheld" is the unsafe
upper bound: the body is removed from the transaction, header/URI rules still
run.

| body | full CRS p50 | withheld p50 | speedup | full p95 | withheld p95 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 KiB | 22.6 ms | 2.1 ms | 10.7× | 70.9 ms | 2.9 ms |
| 4 KiB | 80.8 ms | 1.5 ms | 53.2× | 81.5 ms | 3.8 ms |
| 8 KiB | 155.3 ms | 1.7 ms | 91.9× | 217.7 ms | 3.2 ms |
| 16 KiB | 379.0 ms | 3.0 ms | 128.0× | 438.1 ms | 4.5 ms |
| 60 KiB | 706.0 ms | 2.0 ms | 354.7× | 734.3 ms | 5.0 ms |

The withheld path is ~2-5 ms regardless of size: it is the fixed CRS skeleton
(phase 1, header rules, blocking evaluation) with no body work. The gap is the
entire ~7.5 µs/byte operator cost. This is the prize, not a number the stock
artifact can claim, because `all_body_rules_gated` is false.

### 4.3 What a per-rule integration would save

The prefilter's gated set covers 62 of 113 body-relevant entries. A per-rule
integration would remove those rules from the transaction and keep the 51
ungated ones (libinjection, size/validation, the 932 generated regexes, short
keyword branches). It would not reach the withheld-path numbers, but it would
remove the gated share of the operator work without changing a decision. The
exact share requires the sidecar `RemoveRuleByID` integration and is the next
measurement to take.

## 5. Detection parity

Corpus: 15 benign bodies and 36 attack bodies
(`tests/corpus/crs-prefilter-corpus.json`). Ground truth is the actual
full-CRS decision from the pinned sidecar.

* **Prefilter hit rate on benign bodies: 7/15 (46.7 %).** The hits are all
  common-substring false positives, not CRS matches: `933160` contains the
  3-character literal `ord`, which occurs inside `password`/`order`;
  `942350`/`942360` contain short SQL keywords (`as`, `from`, ...) that occur
  in ordinary prose. The prefilter is over-approximating, so this is safe but
  costs the fast path.
* **Prefilter hit rate on attack bodies: 29/36 (80.6 %).** The seven misses are
  exactly the ungated rules (see below).
* **Unsafe body-withholding parity** (withhold whenever the prefilter is
  clean, ignoring the ungated guard): 13 clean cases, **6 false negatives, 0
  false positives**. The six mismatches and the rules that produced them are:

| case | full CRS rule(s) | ungated rule | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sqli-error` | 942151, 942100 | 942151 (short SQL function names), 942100 (`@detectSQLi`) | expected; safe mode runs full CRS |
| `sqli-urlencoded` | 942100 | 942100 (`@detectSQLi`) | expected |
| `rce-subshell` (`cmd=$(id)`) | 932130 | 932130 (command substitution, no literal) | expected |
| `log4shell` | 932130, 933135, 944150 | 933135/944150 (short/no literal) | expected |
| `php-object-injection` | 933170 | 933170 (serialized-object regex, no literal) | expected |
| `json-unicode` (benign) | 920540 | 920540 (JSON processor check) | **CRS false positive**, not a prefilter unsoundness |

`json-unicode` is a benign JSON body with `\u00fc` escapes. The sidecar's
Coraza build does not recognise the JSON body processor, so CRS rule 920540
(`REQBODY_PROCESSOR !@streq JSON` chained with a `\uXXXX` search) blocks it.
The prefilter's clean result is arguably the correct one, but the acceptance
gate counts any full-CRS block as ground truth, so it is reported as a
mismatch. In the production `BodyWithhold` mode 920540 is ungated and forces
full CRS, so the request is still blocked exactly as before.

The two attack cases that full CRS *allows* (`rce-backtick`, `ssti-jinja`) are
not parity failures; they are listed only as prefilter misses because the
corpus labels them as attacks.

**Safe-mode parity is 100 % by construction.** With the stock artifact
`all_body_rules_gated == false`, `BodyWithhold` never withholds, so every
request runs full CRS and every decision is identical. The unsafe numbers
above quantify what the ungated rules would cost; they are the reason the
mode refuses to take that path.

## 6. Remaining risks

1. **`@detectSQLi` / `@detectXSS`.** libinjection has no required literal. A
   sound character-class gate exists for XSS (`<` is necessary) but the SQLi
   gate ("contains a digit or punctuation") fires on almost every structured
   body, so it is not useful. The only sound way to skip these rules is to run
   them (they are ~0.1 % of cost) while removing the *gated* rules from the
   transaction.
2. **Gapped literals (932250/932260).** A future extractor can emit
   "subsequence" gates (`b…u…s…y…b…o…x` with bounded gaps) for the generated
   command regexes. That is a different matcher, not a literal set.
3. **Short branches (942151, 942140).** Rules that include 2-character SQL
   function names or DB names cannot be gated on a ≥3-character literal without
   hitting benign text. Lowering the minimum literal length trades hit rate for
   coverage; the artifact records the minimum.
4. **`htmlEntityDecode` fidelity.** Until the full Go HTML5 entity table is
   ported, rules using it are ungated. This is conservative, not unsound.
5. **Artifact/engine skew.** The prefilter is embedded in the Rust binary. If a
   future integration lets the sidecar remove rules, both sides must load the
   same artifact (hash or handshake version check).
6. **XML DTD.** The `<!DOCTYPE`/`<!ENTITY` trigger is a coarse structural
   fallback. A body that hides an entity expansion without those tokens is not
   possible in XML, but non-XML bodies containing those strings take the slow
   path unnecessarily.

## 7. Recommended integration

> **Status: implemented.** The body-withholding mode remains available for
> measurement, but production gating is per-rule
> (`waf.coraza.prefilter = "gated"`). The steps below describe what landed and
> why.

The body-withholding mode is the wrong integration for stock CRS because the
ungated rules must still see the body. The integration is **per-rule gating**:

1. The prefilter returns the set of gated rule ids that *did not* match (all of
   them on a clean body) after scanning the URI, query, headers, cookies and
   body.
2. The native sidecar calls `tx.RemoveRuleByID(id)` for each before
   `ProcessURI` (Coraza already supports this through `ctl`).
3. The wasm reactor has the same list in its ABI; the guest validates it
   against the embedded artifact copy before applying it.
4. Rules that cannot be gated (libinjection, size/validation checks) still run;
   they are cheap and preserve the decision exactly.

This removes the gated share of the ~7.5 µs/byte operator work without changing
any decision, and it degrades gracefully as the extractor improves.

### Wasm equivalent

The WASI reactor now has the per-rule removal ABI: `remove_rule_ids` in the
JSON payload. The guest embeds `rules/crs/prefilter.json` (a byte-identical
copy of the host artifact, enforced by a unit test), validates every id, and
calls `tx.RemoveRuleByID` before `ProcessURI`. `PrefilterMode::BodyWithhold`
remains as a measurement path and is only valid when `all_body_rules_gated` is
true; `PrefilterMode::DryRun` records the verdict without changing the payload.

## 8. Reproduction

```sh
# Regenerate the artifact and summary.
nix develop -c cargo run --features crs-prefilter --bin crs-prefilter-extract

# Unit tests (including adversarial extraction cases).
nix develop -c cargo test --lib --features crs-prefilter

# Benchmark + parity (needs a running native sidecar).
nix develop -c cargo run --release --features crs-prefilter,coraza-native \
  --bin crs-prefilter-bench -- --socket /tmp/opencode/coraza.sock --reps 3
```
